passage: I'm Mehak, and I go to Sunday class at the community hall with my friend Disha. Our religious teacher tells stories, and Disha listens with her chin on her hands and does not blink. Last week the story was about a man who fed hungry animals in the rain. All the way home Disha told it to me again, sure that every part happened exactly as told. This week the story was about a punishment for children who miss prayers. Disha went very quiet. She said she would ask her mother about it. I could not tell if it was still bothering her by evening.

qa.q: Where do Mehak and Disha go on Sundays?
qa.a: They go to Sunday class at the community hall.

qa.q: What did Disha seem to feel about the stories, and what changed with the punishment story?
qa.a: She seemed to trust the stories completely, but the punishment story made her very quiet and probably worried, though Mehak could not be sure what she was thinking.

qa.q: What could Disha do about the story that unsettled her?
qa.a: Ask her mother, as she said she would, and notice how stories about kindness feel different from stories that only frighten.

qa.q: How might the religious teacher see Disha in class?
qa.a: As an attentive child who takes the stories in fully; the teacher may not know that one story worried her.

grounding: Illustrates a child fully trusting a religious teacher's stories, with a first small sign of noticing a frightening one.

passage: Every Sunday in Cape Town, Camila sat cross-legged in the church hall while Brother Thabo told stories: a shepherd searching all night for one lost sheep, a stranger stopping to help a hurt man on the road. Camila believed every word. She loved how his voice went soft at the sad parts. One Sunday a visiting speaker came instead and said children who asked questions would be punished. Camila's stomach went tight. That night she told her mum. 'Brother Thabo never says scary things. He says God is like the shepherd.' Mum hugged her. 'Good noticing. Good teachers make you kinder, not frightened. And you can always ask me.' The next Sunday Brother Thabo was back, and Camila asked him why the shepherd didn't give up. He smiled.

qa.q: What did the shepherd search for all night?
What was Camila feeling when the visiting speaker talked about punishment?
qa.a: Frightened and uneasy; her stomach went tight.

qa.q: What did Camila learn to notice about teachers of faith?
qa.a: That good teachers make you kinder, not frightened, and that she can ask her mum about anything worrying.

qa.q: How did Mum see Camila telling her?
qa.a: As good noticing; she hugged her and invited her always to ask.

grounding: A girl who trusts her Sunday school teacher's stories begins to notice that good teaching promotes kindness, not fear.

passage: Every Saturday morning, Binita went to the children's class at the community temple hall, where Lokesh-ji told stories from the Ramayana with his hands flying. Binita believed every word: the flying monkey, the stones floating on the sea. Afterwards he always asked, 'So what did we learn about being kind?' and everyone had to give one small idea, like sharing tiffin or helping at home. Once Binita put her hand up and asked, 'But why did the stones float?' Some kids laughed. Lokesh-ji didn't. 'Good question. What do you think?' He never asked the children to keep secrets from their parents, and he never made anyone scared. Binita trusted him the way she trusted the morning sun. Walking home, she told Papa her one small idea: helping Nani with the washing.

qa.q: How did Binita feel about Lokesh-ji?
qa.a: Trusting and safe, the way she trusted the morning sun.

qa.q: What signs showed Lokesh-ji's teaching was healthy?
qa.a: He asked about kindness, welcomed questions, and never asked for secrets or made anyone scared.

qa.q: How did Lokesh-ji respond when kids laughed at Binita's question?
qa.a: He didn't laugh; he called it a good question and asked what she thought.

grounding: A girl trusts her temple class teacher, whose teaching invites kindness and questions and never fear or secrecy.
